content: The implementation of new initiatives in hospitals often places a significant burden on resources and time, detracting from the ability to focus on effective execution. When considering monitoring processes, it is essential to collect as much information as possible from program team interactions with participants, whether through webinars, large meetings, or coaching visits. Local implementation teams should be encouraged to administer culture surveys and observe the performance of the Checklist in operating rooms (ORs), sharing the results with the partnership team. Additionally, it is important to explore how existing monitoring processes can be leveraged to collect relevant information. At the facility level, implementing any type of change is inherently challenging and requires time. Even seemingly simple and intuitive projects can be difficult to execute because they necessitate changes in how individuals perform their jobs and behave. For example, while implementing the Checklist at the facility level may appear straightforward, it often requires OR team members to alter their workflows, use unfamiliar tools, and adopt new communication practices. Although the concept of the Checklist is simple, its execution demands a significant cultural shift within hospital settings, requiring time, effort, and persistence. Facilities have reported several challenges during implementation. In some cases, the Checklist was no longer in use after the initial implementation effort, often due to a lack of ongoing support and encouragement for its continued use. Even when the Checklist was being used, there was room for improvement in its application. Successful implementation requires a gradual, stepwise approach, starting small and building consensus across the organization over time. Facilities that imposed rigid deadlines for universal adoption without adequate preparation often faced resistance and failure. Misuse or underuse of the Checklist, lack of buy-in from clinicians (especially surgeons), and insufficient leadership support were common barriers. To address these challenges, a structured implementation pathway is recommended. This involves several key steps: 1. Recruit a Team: Assemble a multidisciplinary team responsible for planning and executing the implementation. This team should include representatives from all OR roles and at least one administrative representative. 2. Understand the Work: The implementation team must have a thorough understanding of the Checklist, as they will need to teach and coach colleagues while addressing questions about its purpose, evidence, and benefits. 3. Assess the Environment: Evaluate current practices, staff perceptions of safety and teamwork, and the facility’s culture through surveys and observations. This information will guide the development of a tailored implementation plan. 4. Pause and Reflect: Analyze the data collected during the assessment phase to determine the facility’s readiness to proceed. Present findings and proposed plans to leadership, seeking their support. 5. Customize and Test: Modify the Checklist to meet the facility’s specific needs. Test any changes outside the OR (e.g., in simulation settings) before using the Checklist with patients. 6. Plan Expansion: Develop a detailed plan for expanding Checklist use within the facility. Start small and build gradually, remaining flexible to adapt the plan as needed. 7. Engage Through 1-on-1 Conversations: Personal conversations are critical for connecting individuals to the purpose of the Checklist and securing their support. Every OR team member should be engaged in this way before using the Checklist. 8. Promote the Checklist: Raise awareness and foster a sense of shared mission through internal publicity efforts, such as videos, newsletters, and bulletin boards. However, promotion should complement, not replace, personal engagement. 9. Train and Spread: Provide training to surgical team members on how to properly use the Checklist. This includes demonstrations and opportunities to practice in non-clinical settings. 10. Watch and Coach: Coaching is essential for sustaining effective Checklist use and improving team performance over time. It builds on the foundation of personal conversations and hands-on training. 11. Continually Improve: Sustaining and improving the Checklist’s use requires ongoing engagement with surgical teams, regular coaching, and annual culture surveys. The implementation team should remain active, with periodic changes in membership and updates to the Checklist to reflect evolving organizational needs. In resource-constrained settings, such as lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), additional challenges arise. Governments often lack the resources to support implementation, and facilities may have limited infrastructure for quality improvement. In many cases, the Checklist was observed in facilities but not actively used. To address these issues, it is critical to emphasize how the Checklist can be implemented without requiring new resources. For example, adapting workflows to ensure antibiotics are administered within the recommended timeframe can significantly improve outcomes without additional costs. The Checklist’s design as a universal template allows it to be adapted to diverse surgical settings. It prompts teams to discuss plans, address concerns, verify critical information, and confirm the completion of essential processes. Even partial implementation of the Checklist can yield benefits and serve as a starting point for broader adoption. In LMICs, success often depends on strong clinical champions and external support. Programs like Lifebox’s “Clean Cut” initiative have demonstrated the value of using the Checklist to engage surgical teams, monitor data, and align practices with infection prevention standards. Clean Cut focuses on six key perioperative standards, including skin antisepsis, sterile field maintenance, instrument sterility, antibiotic timing, surgical swab tracking, and verbal “time-outs” before incision. By mapping upstream steps and identifying barriers, this program facilitates the development of contextually relevant solutions. Ultimately, the implementation process itself can drive cultural change within organizations, fostering a quality improvement infrastructure for future initiatives. A multidisciplinary, stepwise approach aligned with WHO recommendations is essential for success. Even if full implementation is not immediately feasible, incremental steps can pave the way for eventual adoption. Sustained efforts to disseminate and implement the Checklist should continue, as its potential to improve surgical safety is significant.
